authors: Samuel De Lemos, Giacomo Loi, Mentor Mehmedi, Rudi Becker Đuricic (EGOV), Andras Schwarcz, Anda-Diana Ghiran-Merveille, Ludovica Munari (BSU), European Parliament
title: Recovery and Resilience Dialogue with the European Commission: BUDG-ECON Committee meeting on 9 February 2026 (In-depth analysis, PE 779.862)
venue: European Parliament, Economic Governance and EMU Scrutiny Unit (EGOV) and Budgetary Support Unit
method: descriptive statistics from the Commission's RRF Scoreboard (absorption, milestones, plan revisions) plus country case notes
outcomes: disbursement and absorption rates, milestone fulfilment, reasons for plan amendments
headline: By end-January 2026, 66% of RRF grants and 77% of loans had been disbursed, but cutting eight countries' loan envelopes alone raised the Facility-wide absorption rate from 60.5% to 68.3%, and 57% of plan amendments since June 2025 cited 'administrative simplification' (vs 15% before).
summary_plain: Parliament's own analysts show that much of the recent 'progress' in spending EU recovery money comes from countries shrinking the loans they asked for, not from faster delivery, and that late plan changes increasingly water down commitments.
quality: Official descriptive monitoring based on public Scoreboard data; no causal analysis; useful decomposition of absorption figures.

authors: Manuel Hidalgo, Jorge Galindo, Javier Martínez (EsadeEcPol)
title: Evolución de los Fondos Next-Gen EU en España (EsadeEcPol Policy Brief #55)
method: descriptive statistics from the EsadeEcPol NextGenEU Tracker (calls, awards and beneficiaries of Spain's recovery plan, data to 12 March 2026)
outcomes: funds called vs awarded, regional and sectoral distribution, concentration of beneficiaries
headline: Spain had called EUR 90.7bn in RRF grants but awarded only EUR 63.4bn by March 2026 (a EUR 27bn gap), and the top 1% of beneficiaries received 71.4% of the value awarded, with construction taking over EUR 13bn versus about EUR 1.3bn for education and health combined.
summary_plain: A Spanish think tank tracking the EU recovery money finds that a large share was still not awarded months before the deadline, and that most of what was awarded went to a small number of big recipients and to building works rather than skills or health.
quality: Careful administrative-data tracker; descriptive only; awards are not the same as spending or impact.

authors: Área financiera y digitalización de Funcas
title: Fondos NextGen: ¿la transformación que no llega? (Cuadernos de Información Económica, n.º 308)
method: descriptive analysis of budget execution data for Spain's Recovery, Transformation and Resilience Plan
outcomes: commitments vs actual payments, share of current vs investment spending
headline: By mid-2025 fewer than one third of Spain's NextGen budget credits had turned into actual payments, and about 25% of resources went to current rather than investment spending.
summary_plain: Spain was quick to sign up for and receive EU recovery money, but slow to actually spend it, and a quarter went on day-to-day costs rather than long-term investment, so the promised transformation of the economy has been limited.
quality: Descriptive budget-execution analysis by an established think tank; abstract and introduction read; no counterfactual.
interested_party: Funcas is the research foundation of the Spanish savings-bank confederation (CECA)

title: The Post-DSM Copyright Report
method: comparative legal mapping of more than 500 national provisions implementing the DSM Directive in all EU Member States, with accompanying database
outcomes: transposition of user-rights provisions (TDM, education, cultural heritage, Art. 7 override protection, press publishers' right limits, Art. 17 safeguards)
headline: Twenty Member States adopted research exceptions broader than the Directive's mandatory TDM exception, but many failed to fully implement mandatory limits on the press publishers' right and most took a minimalist approach to Article 17 user safeguards.
summary_plain: A review of how every EU country wrote the 2019 copyright rules into national law finds that countries went in very different directions: many widened rights for researchers, but protections for ordinary users against over-blocking and limits on publishers' new rights were often left out.
quality: Systematic, transparent legal mapping; measures legal outputs, not economic or behavioural effects; author organisation advocates for user rights.
interested_party: Campaigning association for the public domain and user rights in copyright

title: Our experiment on the value of European news content (with EU 2025 Report on the Value of News Content)
method: randomised experiment: EU-publisher news removed from Search, News and Discover for 1% of users in eight Member States, 14 Nov 2024 to 31 Jan 2025
outcomes: Google Search ad revenue, Google usage
headline: Removing EU news publishers' content for 1% of users produced no measurable change in Google Search ad revenue and a 0.8% drop in usage.
summary_plain: Google ran a test hiding European news from a small share of users to argue, in payment talks under the press publishers' right, that news brings it little advertising money; it reports no measurable revenue loss.
period_geography: Belgium, Croatia, Denmark, Greece, Italy, Netherlands, Poland, Spain; Nov 2024 to Jan 2025
quality: Randomised design but run and reported by the party paying under Art. 15; short horizon, 1% sample, ignores publisher-side value; Google says an external firm (Coalfire) checked execution.
interested_party: Google is the main licensee under Article 15 and is negotiating payments with publishers

authors: Autorità per le garanzie nelle comunicazioni (AGCOM)
title: Regolamento (UE) 2019/1150 - Report sull'attività di monitoraggio 2023
method: survey of business users and corporate website owners plus information requests and review of platforms' and search engines' terms and conditions (Feb-Jun 2023, second annual round)
outcomes: business-user awareness, complaint handling, mediation use, compliance of T&Cs
headline: About 86% of Italian business users had no or only superficial knowledge of the P2B Regulation, 68% found platforms' complaint systems hard to access and only 15% of complaints succeeded, while about 60% of platforms updated their T&Cs and 93% named mediators.
summary_plain: Italy's communications regulator found that online platforms have largely updated their terms to follow the EU platform-to-business rules, but most small firms do not know their rights and find platforms' complaint channels unhelpful.
quality: Official monitoring with survey and document review; self-selected survey respondents (sample size not stated in summary); descriptive.

authors: Peiyao Ma, Andrea Mantovani, Carlo Reggiani, Annette Broocks, Néstor Duch-Brown
title: The Price Effects of Banning Price Parity Clauses in the EU: Evidence from International Hotel Groups
venue: TSE Working Paper 1371 (Toulouse School of Economics)
method: quasi-experimental difference-in-differences on hotel room prices of three international hotel groups around the 2015 French ban (validated with Germany 2016 and Austria 2017 bans)
headline: The full removal of price parity clauses in France in 2015 had a limited and non-significant effect on room prices, with similar results for Germany and Austria.
summary_plain: Banning the contract terms that stopped hotels offering cheaper rooms outside booking platforms did not noticeably lower the prices consumers paid.
quality: Predecessor evidence: national parity bans before VBER 2022 (which removed wide parity clauses from the block exemption); credible DiD but limited to three hotel groups; co-authors at the Commission's JRC.

title: Submission to the European Commission's post-adoption consultation on Combating online child sexual abuse - amending temporary derogation from certain provisions of Directive 2002/58/EC
method: structured critique of the Commission's 2023 implementation report and provider transparency data (re-analysis of reported error rates)
outcomes: evidence of necessity/effectiveness, false-positive rates of detection tools
headline: Using the only provider that reported actual error rates under the Regulation, EDRi shows LinkedIn's automated tools flagged 75 items of which only 31 were confirmed as CSAM in 2021, a 59% false-positive rate, versus the 99.9% accuracy cited by the Commission.
summary_plain: A digital-rights network argues that the Commission's own report on the temporary scanning rules contains no solid evidence that scanning private messages has helped protect children, and that the little real data available shows many false alarms.
quality: Secondary analysis of official report data; very small sample for the error-rate figure; written by a campaigning organisation.
interested_party: Campaigning digital-rights NGO network opposed to CSAM scanning of private communications

authors: Paul Bouchaud, Marc Faddoul, Raziye Buse Çetin (AI Forensics)
title: No Embargo in Sight: Meta lets pro-Russia propaganda ads flood the EU
method: measurement study using Meta's DSA Art. 39 ad repository: language-model classifier (AUC 0.95, 3,000+ hand-labelled ads) applied to 30 million ads in 16 EU countries, plus manual annotation of 100 moderated and 100 declared ads per country
outcomes: share of political ads undeclared, moderation recall and precision, reach of coordinated scam/propaganda networks
headline: An estimated 66% of political ads on Meta in 16 EU countries were not declared as such and Meta moderated under 5% of them (22.8% in Ireland vs 3.9% in Hungary), while a pro-Russian network of 3,800+ pages reached over 38 million accounts in Aug 2023 to Mar 2024.
summary_plain: Researchers used the ad archive the DSA forces Meta to publish and found that most political ads slip through without being labelled or checked, letting propaganda and scam campaigns reach tens of millions of Europeans.
period_geography: 16 EU Member States, Aug 2023 to Feb 2024
quality: Large-scale measurement with validated classifier; conservative estimates; NGO report not peer reviewed; enabled by DSA transparency rather than measuring a causal DSA effect.
interested_party: Platform-accountability NGO that advocates DSA enforcement against VLOPs

title: Full Disclosure: Stress testing tech platforms' ad repositories
method: compliance audit of 12 VLOP/VLOSE ad repositories (web interfaces and APIs) against DSA Art. 39(1-2) and 20+ criteria, with stress and usability testing, Dec 2023 to Jan 2024
outcomes: completeness, data fields, accessibility and usability of DSA-mandated ad repositories
headline: None of the 12 platforms tested (incl. AliExpress, Apple, Bing, Booking, Google, LinkedIn, Meta, Pinterest, Snapchat, TikTok, X, Zalando) offered a fully functional ad repository; AliExpress had no API and X provided only a CSV file.
summary_plain: An independent test of the public ad archives that the DSA requires big platforms to publish found every one of them incomplete, buggy or hard to use, limiting outside scrutiny of advertising ahead of the 2024 EU elections.
quality: Structured audit with explicit criteria; snapshot in time; qualitative scoring by advocacy organisations.
interested_party: Mozilla Foundation campaigns for platform transparency (its subsidiary Mozilla Corporation competes with some audited firms)

title: Ticked off: TikTok approves EU elections disinformation ads for publication in Ireland
method: audit experiment: 16 election-disinformation video ads submitted to each of TikTok, YouTube and X targeting Ireland (May 2024), withdrawn before publication
headline: TikTok approved 16 of 16 (100%) election-disinformation ads, YouTube approved 2 of 16, and X blocked all and suspended the account.
summary_plain: A campaign group tested whether platforms would accept fake election ads before the 2024 European elections, which the DSA requires them to guard against; TikTok approved every one.
quality: Simple controlled audit with very small sample; one country and one moment; campaigning NGO.
interested_party: Campaigning NGO that filed a DSA complaint against TikTok

authors: Julian Jaursch, Jakob Ohme, Ulrike Klinger
title: Joint paper by the Weizenbaum Institute, European University Viadrina and SNV on data access for researchers under the DSA
method: analysis of early Article 40(12) data-access requests based on researcher conversations and voluntary reports to the DSA40 Data Access Tracker
outcomes: researchers' experiences with VLOP data-access applications (process, response times, rejections)
headline: Early experience with DSA Article 40(12) shows researchers from academia and civil society still face significant hurdles in obtaining publicly accessible VLOP data, despite some platforms' steps toward compliance.
summary_plain: Policy researchers collected early reports from scientists trying to use the DSA's new right to platform data and found the process slow, uneven and often blocked.
quality: Structured assessment from a self-selected tracker sample; landing page only, numbers not verified.

authors: Niklas Eder, Agata Russo (User Rights); Agne Kaarlep, Laura Zurdo, Toshali Sengupta (Tremau)
title: State of Play of DSA Dispute Settlement: Meaningful Redress, Uneven Results
method: descriptive comparison of 2025 transparency reports of five certified Article 21 out-of-court dispute settlement bodies
outcomes: dispute volumes, share of platform decisions overturned, platform implementation of ODS decisions
headline: In User Rights' 2025 data, 84.4% of concluded proceedings found the platform's original decision unjustified, and effective implementation of outcomes was about 90% at TikTok but around 13% at Meta.
summary_plain: Data from the new independent bodies that settle content-moderation disputes under the DSA show users usually win, but whether platforms follow the rulings varies hugely, with Meta rarely complying.
quality: Descriptive synthesis of self-reported ODS data; different reporting periods across bodies; authors run an ODS body and a trust-and-safety consultancy.
interested_party: Authors from User Rights (a certified ODS body) and Tremau (DSA compliance vendor)

authors: European Board for Digital Services and European Commission
title: Second report on systemic risks on very large online platforms and search engines under the Digital Services Act (Article 35(2) DSA)
venue: European Commission, Shaping Europe's digital future
method: structured qualitative mapping of systemic risks and mitigation measures reported by or observed on VLOPs/VLOSEs (risk assessments, audits, stakeholder input), 17 Feb 2025 to 16 Feb 2026
outcomes: prominent systemic risks and platforms' mitigation measures
headline: The second annual Article 35(2) report identifies risks to minors (grooming, harmful content, addictive design, AI-generated sexual content) as most prominent and declines to label any platform mitigation measure as 'best practice'.
summary_plain: The EU's annual overview of risks on the biggest platforms says protecting children is the top concern and that the DSA's risk-management system is still at an early stage.
quality: Official structured assessment, largely qualitative; regulator assessing its own regime; landing page and secondary summary (eucrim) read.
interested_party: Commission and Board assessing the regime they enforce

title: Umsetzungsstand EU-Verordnung zum Single Digital Gateway zum 31.12.2024 in Deutschland (Beschluss 2025/21)
method: descriptive monitoring statistics: compliance dashboard of 16,677 service descriptions, user feedback (36,021 ratings), online availability of Annex II procedures
outcomes: information quality, user satisfaction, online availability of SDG procedures, Your Europe usage
headline: At end-2024, only 22% of Germany's 16,677 SDG-relevant service descriptions fully met requirements (29% not at all), users rated SDG services 2.95 of 5 stars on average, and 18 of 19 required procedures were online but only one federal-state service was available nationwide.
summary_plain: Germany's federal-state IT council reports that a year after the EU deadline, most required online government procedures exist, but information is often incomplete, users are lukewarm and availability across regions is patchy.
quality: Official administrative monitoring; descriptive; one Member State.

searched: Think-tank/consultancy sweep (BEUC, CERRE, WIK, ETNO, GSMA, Copenhagen Economics, Analysys Mason) and roaming traffic/wholesale cap evidence; only pre-2022 RLAH material, existing BEREC/Commission reports, or blocked pages (UKE Poland analysis, Analysys Mason summary) found.

Evaluation/effectiveness studies, Eurojust/Europol statistics, think-tank assessments, and the Article 21(2) impact evaluation due 31 May 2026 (EUR-Lex search); only the existing 2023 compliance report and monitoring programme SWD(2023) 23 (not an evaluation) found.
